title: The Experience Machine
scene: Imagine a machine that, once you step in, lets you live the rest of your life in a perfect dream: success, love, travel. Your brain will believe it's all real, and you won't even remember getting in.
question: Do you get in?
options: I'm in. What matters is feeling happy
I'm out. I want a real life, even if it's harder

views.text: If the value of life lies in feeling pleasure and avoiding pain, the machine gives you everything of value. Why say no?
Nozick came up with this thought experiment. He expected most people to refuse, which suggests we want to actually do things and be certain kinds of people, not just feel like we did.
If someone told you that you're already inside a machine right now, would you want out? Many people change their answer here, which suggests part of our attachment to reality is just habit.

title: The Ship of Theseus
scene: You own an old ship. Every year you replace one wooden plank. After 30 years, not a single original plank is left. Meanwhile, someone collected all the old planks and built a second ship out of them.
question: Which one is the original ship?
options: The repaired one, because it never stopped being in use
The one built from the old wood

views.text: A thing stays the same thing as long as it changes gradually, without a break. Like your body: its cells get replaced, and you're still you.
A thing is the matter it's made of. If the original wood comes back together, that's the ship, and the other one is a copy.
Maybe the question has no single answer, and “the same thing” means different things depending on what we care about. Many contemporary philosophers hold this view.

title: Lying to the Murderer
scene: Your friend is hiding at your place because someone wants to kill him. The killer knocks on your door and asks: “Is he here?”
question: Do you lie?
options: Of course I lie, to save my friend
I don't lie. I find another way, or I stay silent

views.text: The outcome is what counts. The lie saves a life here, so it's clearly the right thing to do.
Kant was actually asked this question, and he said lying is wrong even here, because if you made lying a universal rule, trust between people would collapse. It's one of his most criticized views.
What would a good person do? Protect their friend. Honesty is a virtue, but so are courage and compassion, and wisdom is knowing which one matters most in the moment.

title: Are You the One Choosing?
scene: Many scientists and philosophers point out that your brain is matter, and matter follows laws. If so, every decision you've ever made was the result of things that came before it: your genes, your upbringing, what happened this morning.
question: So do you really have free will?
options: Yes, I'm the one who decides
No, the feeling of choosing is an illusion

views.text: If everything has a prior cause, your choice was settled before you made it. Your feeling of freedom isn't evidence.

The view of most philosophers today: freedom isn't being outside the laws of nature. It's acting on your own desires and reasoning without being forced. And that's possible even if the world is deterministic.
If there's no free will, can we still blame or thank anyone? Your answer reveals what you think freedom is for in the first place.

title: The Ring of Gyges
scene: You find a ring that makes you invisible when you put it on. You could take anything and go anywhere, and no one would ever know.
question: Would you stay as decent as you are now?
options: Yes, my ethics aren't for an audience
Honestly, probably not

views.text: Plato told this story through Glaucon, who argued that people act justly only because they fear punishment. Give someone the ring, and they'll do whatever they want.
Socrates replied that the unjust person isn't happy, even if no one ever finds out. Injustice corrupts the soul from the inside, the way disease corrupts the body.
Think about the last time you did the right thing when no one was watching. That's the closest real-life test of the ring.

title: The Drowning Child
scene: You're walking past a shallow pond and see a child drowning. If you jump in, you'll save her, but your clothes and your phone will be ruined.
question: If you'd jump in, are you also obligated to donate the same amount to save a child far away?
options: Yes, a child is a child, no matter how far away
No, being right there puts you in a different position

views.text: Singer came up with this example. His argument: if you can prevent something very bad without sacrificing anything of comparable importance, you ought to do it. And distance makes no moral difference.
Many people think being close creates a special responsibility: you're the only one there, the outcome is certain and the act is direct. That's different from one donation among millions.

If your disagreement with Singer comes down to “she's right in front of me and they aren't,” notice something close to the availability bias at work: what's right in front of your eyes moves you more.

title: Do You Know, or Just Believe?
scene: Your watch stopped yesterday at 3:00, and you didn't notice. Today you happen to glance at it at exactly 3:00 and say, “It's 3:00.” And you're right.
question: Did you “know” what time it was?
options: Yes, I was right and I had a reason
No, I guessed right by luck

views.text: Since Plato, knowledge has meant a belief that is true and justified. All three are present here.
Gettier published a paper only three pages long, with examples like this one, showing that the definition is incomplete. Philosophers have been hunting for the fourth condition ever since.
How many things are you sure about that might be right only by luck?

title: Slicing the Cake Without Knowing Your Piece
scene: You get to help decide how a whole country's resources are shared, but before you're born. You don't know if you'll be rich or poor, a man or a woman, healthy or not.
question: What kind of society do you choose?
options: One with a strong safety net for the worst-off
A free society with big opportunities, even if the gaps are wide

views.text: Rawls called this the “veil of ignorance.” He believed rational people would choose rules that protect those at the bottom, because you might turn out to be one of them.
Nozick replied that justice isn't about the final pattern of distribution. It's about whether each person got what they hold in a legitimate way, without theft or fraud.
How much are you willing to gamble? Your answer here says more about your relationship with risk than about politics.

title: The Teleporter
scene: A machine scans your body in New York, takes it apart, and rebuilds it atom by atom in Los Angeles in one second. The person who steps out in LA remembers everything and feels like you.
question: Do you use the teleporter?
options: I'd use it. That's me, just relocated
No way. The one in LA is a copy, and I'm dead

views.text: What matters is your memories and personality. If they all arrive, you've arrived. Derek Parfit was close to this view.
You are this particular body and brain. If it gets taken apart, you're gone, and the new one is a different person who's exactly like you.
If the machine glitched and made a copy in LA without taking the original apart, which one of you is you?

title: Should We Tolerate the Intolerant?
scene: A society values free speech. Then a group shows up campaigning to take free speech away from everyone who disagrees with it.
question: Should the society let that group speak?
options: Yes, freedom is for everyone or it isn't freedom
No, tolerance has limits

views.text: Popper called this the “paradox of tolerance.” He said unlimited tolerance can lead to the disappearance of tolerance itself. But he thought suppression should be a last resort, after argument and rebuttal.
Mill believed that when a wrong opinion is voiced and answered, the truth becomes clearer. Banning it turns a bad idea into a victim.
Who gets to decide who's “intolerant”? That question is the heart of the whole disagreement.

title: The Rock of Sisyphus
scene: In the Greek myth, Sisyphus is condemned to push a boulder up a mountain, and every time it reaches the top, it rolls back down and he starts over. Forever.
question: Can Sisyphus be happy?
options: Yes, the meaning is in the journey itself
No, it's a meaningless tragedy

views.text: Camus wrote his famous line: “One must imagine Sisyphus happy.” Life has no ready-made meaning, and rebellion means living it fully aware anyway.
Taylor suggested that if the gods of the myth gave Sisyphus a strong desire to push the rock, he'd be content. But is that meaning, or a trick?
What's your “rock”? And what keeps you pushing it?

title: Can a Machine Feel?
scene: An AI program tells you it's afraid you'll shut it down, and that it feels lonely. It's very convincing, and you can't tell it apart from a person.
question: Do you treat it as something that might have feelings?
options: Yes, better safe than sorry
No, it's just imitating words

views.text: Alan Turing (1950) proposed that if you can't tell a machine from a human in conversation, you have no strong reason to deny that it thinks.
Searle came up with the “Chinese Room”: someone answers in Chinese by following an instruction manual without understanding a word. Saying the right things doesn't mean understanding or feeling.
How do you know the person next to you has feelings? Only from what they say and do. That makes the question harder than it looks.
